sentences.text: The reason there is a book at all is a Thursday in November 1951.

Her great-grandfather was in the yard behind the workshop at about half past three in the afternoon, and it was flat calm — properly flat, the kind of still that happens over that country in November when a high sits on it, with smoke going straight up from every chimney in the town.
He watched it go, in still air, through about a hundred and thirty degrees, from south-west round to north-north-west, taking perhaps forty seconds, and stop.
Forty seconds is the detail that Femke keeps coming back to.
A vane in a gust snaps round.
It goes in a second or two and it overshoots and comes back and hunts about before it settles, because it is a plate on a spindle being hit by moving air.
Forty seconds, smoothly, through a hundred and thirty degrees, with no overshoot and no hunting, is not what a plate on a spindle does when it is hit by anything.
It is what a plate on a spindle does when it is turned.
He went and got two men from the workshop and one of them was the sexton and they stood in the street and looked at it for a quarter of an hour, and nothing else happened.
There was no wind that afternoon or that evening.
Smoke went straight up until dark.

The sexton's name was Aalders and he had the keys and he went up the tower that evening and came down and said that the mechanism was as it always was, which is written into entry two in a different hand.
The wind came in from the north-north-west at about eleven the following morning and blew hard for two days.

That is entry one and it is written in a wheelwright's hand with the time to the nearest quarter hour and both bearings estimated by eye, and underneath it, in the same ink, is the sentence that made Femke sit down on the floor of her grandmother's spare room: *Others have said this.
